A 35-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast cancer (including a sister with a deleterious BRCA1 mutation) is found to carry the same mutation. Which range represents the lifetime risk of breast cancer that should be quoted to her?
D
BRCA1 carriers have a lifetime breast cancer risk of about 60–70% (quoted as 50–80%), with a high risk of ovarian cancer too.
For the same patient with a BRCA1 mutation, which of the following management strategies is an accepted option for her high-risk status?
Yearly self-breast examination|Six-monthly mammography|Bilateral breast irradiation|Prophylactic unilateral mastectomy|Chemoprevention with tamoxifen
E
Options for BRCA carriers are annual MRI (± mammography) surveillance, chemoprevention (tamoxifen) and bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy ± salpingo-oophorectomy; unilateral mastectomy is not enough.

A 47-year-old woman is diagnosed with a unifocal 2.5-cm grade 3 invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast with a clinically and sonographically normal axilla. Following MDT discussion, which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?
A unifocal tumour suitable for breast conservation with a negative axilla: wide local excision with sentinel node biopsy, then radiotherapy and systemic therapy by histology.
Inflammatory breast cancer (dermal lymphatic invasion) is treated with trimodality therapy: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, modified radical mastectomy, then radiotherapy.
Standard regimens are anthracycline–cyclophosphamide followed by a taxane, with trastuzumab/pertuzumab added for HER2-positive disease (e.g. TCHP).
The NHS Breast Screening Programme invites women aged 50 to 70 (up to their 71st birthday) for mammography every 3 years.
A 4-cm node-negative well-differentiated tumour is T2N0 (stage IIA); about 70% 5-year survival in the source (higher with modern adjuvant therapy).
